html:
SMTO-SSH-0004 — SMTO couldn't read the remote computer's security key

GUID: 7c7b5d77-6e34-4aec-a27c-5fc66317c059
Slug: ssh-host-key-invalid
Domain: SSH · Subsystem: ssh

What happened

  • To recognize a computer later, SMTO stores its security key. The key it found was unreadable, of a type SMTO doesn't support, or a certificate rule instead of a plain key, so SMTO couldn't remember this computer. Your command may still have run.

How to fix — simple steps

  1. Check whether the command already did its job on the remote computer before asking SMTO to run it again. SMTO reads this key after the SSH connection is made, so the command may have finished even though the key couldn't be saved.
  2. Ask the person who manages the Gateway computer which key type the remote computer uses. SMTO supports ed25519, RSA and ECDSA keys. Other key types, such as DSA or hardware security-key types, can't be remembered by SMTO.
  3. If the Gateway trusts that computer through a certificate rule, ask them to also add the computer's plain key after confirming it with the computer's manager. SMTO needs a plain, confirmed key to recognize the computer; it doesn't follow certificate rules.

What success looks like

  • After the next SSH command, later commands on that computer run without this message.

If it still fails

  • Select Copy error details and send them to the person who manages the Gateway computer. Don't turn off key checking, and don't trust a key that nobody has confirmed.

Technical details

Observed condition

  • The SSH host key used for pinning is oversized, malformed or of an unsupported algorithm, or the matching known_hosts line is a @cert-authority or @revoked marker rather than a raw public key.

What this means

  • Host-key fingerprinting rejects an oversized/malformed key or unsupported algorithm, or initial known-host lookup finds a marker record rather than a raw public key. Continuity evidence and command outcome are separate. Only the explicit pre-dispatch privilege refusal proves no new execution; observation failure alone cannot prove that a prior SSH command had no effect.

Why this can happen

  • Host-key fingerprinting rejects an oversized/malformed key or unsupported algorithm, or initial known-host lookup finds a marker record rather than a raw public key.

How to diagnose it

  • Distinguish unsupported CA/revocation marker entries from malformed raw key bytes and verify identity independently.

How to fix it

  • fingerprint() accepts only ssh-ed25519, ssh-rsa and ecdsa-sha2-nistp256/384/521 key blobs up to 2048 characters, and Observation._setup rejects known_hosts lines starting with @ (cert-authority or revoked). On the Gateway account, add a raw host-key line for the target, verified through an independent trusted channel, to the known_hosts file OpenSSH names in its 'Found key in' log line. Never disable host verification.
  • Obtain the host’s supported public key through a trusted independent source. Verify its fingerprint before using it for continuity.

Retry and execution caution

  • Correct the recorded cause, then inspect current state and existing receipts before requesting another attempt.

How to verify the fix

  • A trusted supported public host key yields the expected fingerprint without disabling host verification.

What not to do

  • Do not automatically disable certificate verification or trust an unverified replacement identity.

Technical notes

  • Continuity evidence and command outcome are separate. Only the explicit pre-dispatch privilege refusal proves no new execution; observation failure alone cannot prove that a prior SSH command had no effect.
  • Preserve the occurrence ID and safe request/operation references. Receipts and occurrence facts establish what started or completed; the catalog does not authorize retries or establish execution outcome.
